lesson.title: The Shape of All Possible Outcomes
lesson.summary: A distribution organizes the data collected for a variable into a pattern showing what values occur and how often, turning a raw list of numbers into something you can actually read.
lesson.body:
A variable is any characteristic that can be recorded for each individual in a data set, such as eye color, number of siblings, or height. Data are the actual recorded values of that variable for the individuals you observed. A distribution goes one step further than raw data: it describes the overall pattern of a variable by showing what values occur and how often each one occurs. Rather than staring at a long unorganized list of numbers, a distribution organizes that same information so the pattern becomes visible.

Building a distribution requires two things you already have once you know a variable and its data: the set of possible values the variable can take, and a count or proportion of how often each value shows up. This is true whether the variable is categorical, such as favorite subject, or quantitative, such as number of siblings. Once you have both pieces, you can display the distribution in a table or a graph, which are the tools covered in the sections that follow this one.

Consider ten students asked how many siblings they have, giving the data set 0, 1, 1, 2, 0, 1, 3, 1, 2, 1. This list is data: ten individual values of the variable number of siblings. To find the distribution, count how many times each possible value appears. The value 0 appears twice, the value 1 appears five times, the value 2 appears twice, and the value 3 appears once. Checking the total: 2 plus 5 plus 2 plus 1 equals 10, which matches the number of students, confirming every student was counted exactly once.

That summary, 0 siblings for 2 students, 1 sibling for 5 students, 2 siblings for 2 students, and 3 siblings for 1 student, is the distribution of the variable. It answers questions the raw list cannot answer quickly, such as which value is most common, 1 sibling, since 5 is the largest count, and which values are rare, 3 siblings, since only 1 student reported it. The distribution captures the entire pattern of the variable without losing any information about how often each value occurred.

Distributions are the foundation for nearly everything that follows in this course. Frequency tables, relative frequency, cumulative frequency, bar graphs, pie charts, dotplots, stemplots, and histograms are all just different ways of organizing or displaying a distribution, chosen based on whether the variable is categorical or quantitative. Learning to read a distribution, meaning learning to see the pattern of values and their frequencies at a glance, is one of the most important skills in introductory statistics, because nearly every later topic, from shape to center to spread to probability, is really a more precise way of describing a distribution.

It is worth noting that the same variable can produce very different looking distributions depending on the population being studied. The distribution of number of siblings among ten students at one school might look quite different from the distribution among ten students at another school, even though both distributions describe the exact same variable. This is exactly why statisticians rarely trust a conclusion based on a single individual's data value: only by looking at the full distribution, the complete pattern of values and their frequencies, can you tell whether an individual value is typical or unusual within its own group.
